# How Compression and Approximation Affect Efficiency in String Distance Measures

Arun Ganesh<sup>∗</sup>, Tomasz Kociumaka<sup>†</sup>, Andrea Lincoln<sup>†‡</sup>, and Barna Saha<sup>†</sup>

_University of California, Berkeley_

**Abstract**

Real-world data often comes in compressed form. Analyzing compressed data directly (without first decompressing it) can save space and time by orders of magnitude. In this work, we focus on fundamental sequence comparison problems and try to quantify the gain in time complexity when the underlying data is highly compressible. We consider grammar compression, which unifies many practically relevant compression schemes such as the Lempel-Ziv family, dictionary methods, and others. For two strings of total length _N_ and total compressed size _n_, it is known that the edit distance and a longest common subsequence (LCS) can be computed exactly in time \(\widetilde{o}(nN)\), as opposed to _O(N_<sup>2</sup>) for the uncompressed setting. Many real-world applications need to align multiple sequences simultaneously, and the fastest known exact algorithms for median edit distance and LCS of _k_ strings run in _O(N<sup>k</sup>_) time, whereas the one for center edit distance has a time complexity of _O(N_<sup>2_k_</sup>). This naturally raises the question if compression can help to reduce the running time significantly for \(k\ge 3\), perhaps to _O(N_<sup>k/2</sup>_n_<sup>_k/_2</sup>) or, more optimistically, to _O(Nn_<sup>_k_-1</sup>).<sup>1</sup>

Unfortunately, we show new lower bounds that rule out any improvement beyond \(\Omega(N^{k-1}n)\) time for any of these problems assuming the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH), where again _N_ and _n_ represent the total length and the total compressed size, respectively. This answers an open question of Abboud, Backurs, Bringmann, and Künnemann (FOCS’17).

In presence of such negative results, we ask if allowing approximation can help, and we show that approximation and compression together can be surprisingly effective for both multiple and two strings.

We develop an \(\widetilde{o}(N^{k/2}n^{k/2})\)-time FPTAS for the median edit distance of _k_ sequences, leading to a saving of nearly half the dimensions for highly-compressible sequences. In comparison, no \(O(N^{k-\Omega(1)})\)-time PTAS is known for the median edit distance problem in the uncompressed setting. We obtain an improvement from \(\widetilde{o}(N^{2k})\) to \(\widetilde{o}(N^{k/2+o(k)}n^{k/2})\) for the center edit distance problem. For two strings, we get an \(\widetilde{o}(N^{2/3}n^{4/3})\)-time FPTAS for both edit distance and LCS; note that this running time is _o(N_) whenever \(n\checkmark N^{1/4}\). In contrast, for uncompressed strings, there is not even a subquadratic algorithm for LCS that has less than polynomial gap in the approximation factor. Building on the insight from our approximation algorithms, we also obtain several new and improved results for many fundamental distance measures including the edit, Hamming, and shift distances.

### 1 Introduction

With the information explosion, almost all real-world data comes in a compressed form. While compression is primarily intended to save storage space and transmission bandwidth, processing compressed data directly often provides an opportunity to reduce computation time and energy by several orders of magnitude. In this work, we focus on sequential data such as natural-language texts, biological sequences (nucleic acid sequences, including DNA, and amino acid sequences, including proteins), and computer codes. Sequential data often contains highly repetitive pattern. Modern technology (e.g., high-throughput sequencing) has led to an astonishingly rapid accumulation of such data, so much so that without proper data compression and algorithms over compressed data, it is not possible to utilize the wealth of information in them [BPS13, BDY16, PW18, GWH19, HPWO19].

<sup>∗</sup>Supported in part by an NSF 1816861 grant. <sup>†</sup>Supported in part by NSF 1652303, 1909046, and HDR TRIPODS 1934846 grants, and an Alfred P. Sloan Fellowship. <sup>‡</sup>Supported in part by a Simons NTT Research Fellowship. <sup>1</sup>In this paper, we assume that _k_ is a constant; thus, the \(O(\cdot)\) and \(\Omega(\cdot)\) notation may hide factors with exponential dependence on _k_.

Grammar compression represents strings as _straight-line programs_ (SLPs), and provides a mathematically elegant way to unify algorithm design principles for processing compressed data \[Loh12\]. It is equivalent to many well-known compression schemes up to logarithmic factors and moderate constants \[Ryt03, KP18, KK20\] such as the celebrated LZ77 \[ZL77\] and RLBWT \[BW94\] schemes, and at least as strong as byte-pair encoding \[Gag94\], Re-Pair \[LM00\], Sequitur \[NW97\], further members of the Lempel-Ziv family \[ZL78, Wel84\], and many more popular schemes (the list keeps growing). Therefore, following the lead of a large body of previous work (including \[Tis15, Jeż15, ABBK17, BWK19, CKW20\]), we work with grammar-compressed data.

In this work, we ask whether fundamental sequence similarity measures can be computed faster for compressed data. This research is motivated in part by the success of computing edit distance and longest common subsequence (LCS) of two strings \[Gaw12, HLLW13, Tis15\] much faster than the "decompress-and-solve" approach: If we let _N_ denote the total length and _n_ denote the total compressed size of the input strings, then the edit distance and the LCS length can be computed exactly in time \(\widetilde{O}(nN)\) in contrast to _O(N_<sup>2</sup>) time for the uncompressed setting. Therefore, for highly compressible sequences where, say, _n_=pollog_N_, the running time reduces to \(\widetilde{O}(N)\). Abboud, Backurs, Bringmann, and Künnemann \[ABBK17\] asked whether it is possible to improve upon \(\widetilde{O}(nN)\), noting that: "For example, an _O(n_<sup>2</sup>_N_<sup>0.1</sup>) bound could lead to major real-world improvements." In general, any sublinear dependency on _N_ would be preferable; unfortunately, \[ABBK17\] shows that \(\widetilde{O}(Nn)\) is essentially optimal under the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH).

There are many real-world applications which deal with multiple sequences. A survey by Nature \[NMN14\] reports _multiple sequence alignment_ as one of the most used modeling methods in biology, with \[THG94\] among the top-10 papers cited of all time (citation count 63105). Some of the basic measures for multiple sequence similarity include the LCS length and the cost of the median and center strings under edit distance. Abboud, Backurs, and V.-Williams \[ABV15\] showed that exact computation of _k_-LCS requires \(\Omega(N^{k-o(1)})\) time (under SETH), and a similar result has been recently shown for both median and center _k_-edit distance \[HBGT20\]. A simple extension of the basic dynamic programming for two strings solves the median _k_-edit distance problems in _O(N<sup>k</sup>_) time whereas the best bound known for the center _k_-edit distance is _O(N_<sup>2_k_</sup>) \[NR05\]. The two-string lower bound in the compressed setting leaves open the possibility of reducing the running times of the _k_-LCS and the median _k_-edit distance problems for compressed strings: It might be feasible to achieve runtimes of _O(N_<sup>_k/_2</sup>_n_<sup>_k/_2</sup>) or even _O(Nn_<sup>_k_-1</sup>), and a substantial reduction of the exponent at _N_ could lead to significant savings. This raises the following questions:

1. _Does compression allow for significantly reducing the running time for multi-sequence similarity problems?_<tbc>

2. _For the case of two highly compressible strings, what relaxations of the LCS and the edit distance problems could allow circumventing the lower bounds and achieving sublinear dependency on N?_

## Lower Bounds: Compression does not help with exact bounds much!

Unfortunately, we show that computing the _k_-LCS, median _k_-edit distance, and center _k_-edit distance all require \(\Omega((N^{k-1}n)^{1-o(1)})\) time under SETH. Therefore, the potential gain from compression becomes insignificant as _k_ grows. Intuitively, SETH states that CNF-satisfiability requires 2<sup>_n-o(n_)</sup> time \[IP01\]. Even more specifically, we use the _k_-Orthogonal Vectors problem (_k_-OV) \[Vas18\]. At a high level, _k_-OV takes as input a list _L_ with _n_ zero-one vectors of dimension _d_. We must return YES if there exist _k_ vectors that, when multiplied element-wise, form the all zeros vector. The _k_-OV conjecture, which is implied by SETH, states that _k_-OV cannot be solved in \(O(n^{k-\Omega(1)})\) time.

**Theorem 1.1.** _If the_ \(k'\)_-OV hypothesis is true for all constants_ \(k'\)_, then for any constant_ \(\epsilon\in(0,1]\) _grammar-compressed k-LCS requires_ \(\left(N^{k-1}n\right)^{1-o(1)}\) _time when the alphabet size is_ \(|\Sigma|=\Theta(k)\) _and_ \(n=N^{\epsilon\pm o(1)}\)_. Here, N denotes the total length of the k input strings and n is their total compressed size._

We prove similar lower bounds for median and center _k_-edit distance (Theorem 6.5 and Theorem 6.29). Sections 6.2, 6.6, and 6.9 contain our lower bound results.

Abboud, Backurs, Bringmann, and Künnemann \[ABBK17\] left an open question whether their \(\Omega((Nn)^{1-o(1)})\) lower bound for LCS also holds for computing the edit distance of two strings. We answer this question affirmatively and extend the argument to the _k_-string setting. Moreover, we note that for a seemingly simpler problem of computing the shift distance \[AIK08, AIKH13, AGMP13, GKK<sup>+</sup>20\], we show that compression does not help to reduce even a single dimension (Section 8).

## Algorithms: Effectiveness of Approximation & Compression.

In presence of such negative results, relaxing the median and center _k_-edit distance to circumvent the \(\Omega((N^{k-1}n)^{1-o(1)})\) lower bound becomes even more important.

_Can we use compression and approximation together to achieve much better approximation guarantees and, simultaneously, circumvent the exact computation lower bounds?_

To the best of our knowledge, even for two strings, there is no previous work on approximating the edit distance of grammar-compressed strings. On the other hand, even after a long line of research in developing fast algorithms for approximate edit distance for the uncompressed setting (see e.g. \[BEK<sup>+</sup>03, BJKK04, BES06, AKO10, AO12, CDG<sup>+</sup>18, GRS20, BR20, KS20, AN20\]), the best approximation ratio achievable in truly subquadratic time is currently \(3+\epsilon\) \[GRS20\], and the fastest constant-factor approximation algorithm runs in \(O(n^{1+\epsilon})\) time \[AN20\] with an approximation factor that has doubly-exponential dependence on \(\frac{1}{\epsilon}\). The situation is even worse for LCS approximation, where we do not know how to design a subquadratic algorithm with sub-polynomial approximation gap \[HSSS19, RSSS19\]. We are also unaware of any previous research on approximating LCS of two compressed strings.

In the case of multiple strings, there is a classic _O(N_<sup>2</sup>)-time (2-2_/k_)-approximation for median edit distance and an _O(N_<sup>2</sup>)-time 2-approximation for center edit distance \[Gus97\]. Combined with the results of \[AN20\], this yields an \(O(N^{1+\epsilon})\)-time constant-factor approximation for both versions. Nevertheless, a PTAS, that is, a \((1+\epsilon)\)-approximation algorithm for every constant \(\epsilon>0\), would be much more desirable for practical applications.

Surprisingly, we show that already when an \((1+\epsilon)\)-approximation is allowed for an arbitrary constant \(\epsilon>0\), the median _k_-edit distance computation time reduces to \(\widetilde{O}(N^{k/2}n^{k/2})\) compared to the \(\Omega((N^{k-1}n)^{1-o(1)})\) lower bound for exact algorithms. In other words, we can save _k/_2 dimensions by allowing approximation and compression. For \(\epsilon=o(1)\), the running time of our algorithm increases by an \(\epsilon^{-O(k)}\) factor, so we even obtain an FPTAS whereas no prior work in the uncompressed setting gives a \((1+\epsilon)\)-approximation in \(O(N^{k-\Omega(1)})\) time. The reduction in time for center _k_-edit distance is even more dramatic (and technically more complex) from exact _O(N_<sup>2_k_</sup>) to \(\widetilde{O}(N^{k/2+o(k)}n^{k/2})\) for a \((1+\epsilon)\) approximation.

For edit distance between two strings, we develop a more efficient FPTAS whose running time is \(\widetilde{O}(N^{2/3}n^{4/3}\epsilon^{-1/3})\), which is sublinear in _N_ as long as \(n\checkmark N^{1/4}\). A slightly more sophisticated \(\widetilde{O}(N^{2/3}n^{4/3}\epsilon^{-1/3})\)-time algorithm also provides a \((1+\epsilon)\)-approximation of the LCS length. In contrast, a comparable result for the uncompressed setting is an _O(N_<sup>1.95</sup>)-time algorithm of \[RSSS19\], which returns a common subsequence of length \(\Omega(N/\lambda^4)\), providing an \(O(\lambda^3)\)-factor approximation. Even when the alphabet size is 2, so far, there does not exist any \((1+\epsilon)\) approximation in subquadratic time \[RS20\].

## Improved Exact Algorithms in Compressed Setting.

Interestingly, the insights behind our approximation algorithms also lead to new _exact algorithms_. In particular, we show that the edit distance can be computed in time \(\widetilde{O}(n\sqrt{ND})\), where _D_ is an upper bound on the edit distance. This improves upon the state-of-the-art bound of \(\widetilde{O}(min(nN,n+D^2))\) \[Tis15, LV88, MSU97\] whenever \(D\gg N^{1/3}n^{2/3}\).

For this problem, the first improvements compared to the uncompressed settings were given in \[Tis09, HLLW09\]. Then, Tiskin \[Tis15\] obtained an _O(nN_log_N_)-time algorithm and subsequent works \[HLLW13, Gaw12\] reduced the _O_(log_N_) factor. However, when the distance _D_ is small, the edit distance can be computed in _O(N+D_<sup>2</sup>) time \[LV88\] in the uncompressed setting. The _O(N_) term in the running time of the Landau-Vishkin algorithm \[LV88\] is solely needed to construct a data structure efficiently answering the Longest Common Extension (LCE) queries. However, already the results of Mehlhorn, Sundar, and Uhrig \[MSU97\] yield \(\widetilde{O}(1)\)-time LCE queries after \(\widetilde{O}(n)\)-time preprocessing of the grammars representing _X_ and _Y_ . This gives rise to an \(\widetilde{O}(n+D^2)\)-time algorithm computing the edit distance. With a more modern implementation of LCE queries in compressed strings by I \[I17\], the factor hidden within the \(\widetilde{O}(\cdot)\) notation can be reduced to _O_(log_N_).

While the \(\widetilde{O}(n+D^2)\)-time algorithm is very fast if _D_ is small, its efficiency quickly degrades with increasing _D_ and the \(\widetilde{O}(nN)\)-time algorithm becomes more suitable already for \(D\gg\sqrt{nN}\). With a time complexity of \(\widetilde{O}(n\sqrt{ND})\), our algorithm improves upon the previous algorithms whenever \(\sqrt{3}n^2N\checkmark\delta_E(X,Y)\checkmark N\). Nevertheless, the current lower bounds allow for a hypothetical holy-grail algorithm achieving the running time of \(\widetilde{O}(min(nD,n+D^2))\) which we leave as an interesting open question.

We also get improved results for the Hamming distance, which is a more basic measure trivially computable in _O(N_) time. Here, we present an \(O(n\sqrt{N})\)-time algorithm which improves upon the _O(n_<sup>1.41</sup>_N_<sup>0.593</sup>) bound of \[ABBK17\]. Additionally, we note that natural generalizations to multiple strings (including the median Hamming distance) can be computed in _O(nN_<sup>1-1_/k_</sup>) time.

## 2 Preliminaries

For two integers \(i\le j\), we write \[_i...j_\] to denote the set {_i,...,j_} and \[_i...j_) to denote {_i,...,j_-1}. The notions (_i...j_\] and (_i...j_) are defined analogously.

A _string_ is a sequence of characters from a fixed alphabet \(\Sigma\). We write \(\Sigma^*\) to denote the set of all strings over \(\Sigma\), and we define \(\Sigma^+=\Sigma^*\backslash\{\gamma\}\), where \(\gamma\) denotes the empty string. The length of a string _X_ is denoted by |_X_| and, for a position \(i\in[1..|X|]\) in _X_, the character of _X_ at position _i_ is denoted by _X_\[_i_\]. For an integer \(N\ge 0\), the set of length-_N_ strings over \(\Sigma\) is denoted by \(\Sigma^N\).

For two positions \(i\le j\) in _X_, we write _X_\[_i...j_\] to denote the fragment of _X_ starting at positions _i_ and ending at position _j_; this fragment is an occurrence of \(X[i]\cdots X[j]\) as a substring of _X_. The fragments _X_\[_i...j_\], _X(i...j_\], and _X(i...j_) are defined similarly.

A morphism is a function \(f:\Sigma_1^*\rightarrow\Sigma_2^*\) such that \(f(X)=\circlearrowleft_{i=1}^{|X|}f(X[i])\), where \(\circlearrowleft\) denotes the concatenation operator. Note that every function mapping \(\Sigma_1\) to \(\Sigma_2^*\) can be uniquely extended to a morphism.

### 2.1 Straight-Line Programs

A straight-line program is a tuple \(\mathbf{G}=(\mathbf{S},\Sigma,\text{rhs},S)\), where **S** is a finite sequence of _symbols_, \(\Sigma\subseteq\mathbf{S}\) is a set of _terminal symbols_, \(\text{rhs}:(\mathbf{S}\backslash\Sigma)\rightarrow\mathbf{S}^*\) is the _production_ (or _right-hand side_) function, and \(S\in\mathbf{S}\) is the start symbol, and the symbols in **S** are ordered so that _B_ precedes _A_ if _B_ occurs in rhs(_A_). We also write \(A\rightarrow B_1\cdots B_k\) instead of \(\text{rhs}(A)=B_1\cdots B_k\).

The set \(\mathbf{S}\backslash\Sigma\) of _non-terminals_ is denoted by **N**. The size of **G** is \(|\mathbf{G}|:=|\mathbf{S}|+\sum_{A\in\mathbf{N}}|\text{rhs}(A)|\): the number of symbols plus the total length of productions. The _expansion_ function \(\mathrm{exp}:\mathbf{S}\rightarrow\Sigma^+\) is defined recursively:

\(\mathrm{exp}(A)=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
A & \text{if}A\in\Sigma, \\
\circlearrowleft_{i=1}^k\mathrm{exp}(B_i) & \text{if}A\rightarrow\circlearrowleft_{i=1}^kB_i.
\end{array}\right.\)

We say that **G** is a _grammar-compressed representation_ of exp(_S_). The exp function naturally extends to a morphism \(\mathrm{exp}:\mathbf{S}^*\rightarrow\Sigma^*\) with \(\mathrm{exp}(\circlearrowleft_{i=1}^mA_i)=\circlearrowleft_{i=1}^m\mathrm{exp}(A_i)\).

For a symbol \(A\in\mathbf{S}\), we denote |_A_|=|exp(_A_)|. In this work, we assume a word RAM machine with machine words of \(\Omega(\mathrm{log}|S|)\) bits. In this setting, one can compute |_A_| for all \(A\in\mathbf{S}\) in _O_(|**G**|) time. Consequently, we assume that |_A_| is stored along with _A_ in the straight-line programs given to our algorithms.

A straight-line program **G** is in _Chomsky normal form_ if |rhs(_A_)|=2 for all \(A\in\mathbf{N}\). Given an arbitrary straight-line program **G**, an equivalent straight-line program \(\mathbf{G}'\) in Chomsky normal form can be constructed in _O_(|**G**|) time; moreover, \(|\mathbf{G}|=O(|\mathbf{G}'|)\). Thus, without loss of generality, we assume that all straight-line programs given to our algorithms are already in the Chomsky normal form.

## 3 FPTAS for Compressed Edit Distance of Two Strings

The edit distance \(\delta_E(X,Y)\) of two strings \(X,Y\in\Sigma^*\) is defined as the minimum number of character insertions, deletions, and substitutions needed to transform _X_ into _Y_ .

In this section, we prove the following result.

**Theorem 3.1.** _Given a straight-line program_ **G**_<sub>X</sub> of size n generating a string X of length N\>_0_, a straight-line program_ **G**_<sub>Y</sub> of size m generating a string Y of length M\>_0_, and a parameter_ \(\epsilon\in(0,1]\)_, an integer between_ \(\delta_E(X,Y)\) _and_ \((1+\epsilon)\delta_E(X,Y)\) _can be computed in_ \(\bar{O}\left((nm(N+M))^{2/3}\epsilon^{-1/3}\right)\) _time._

Let \(\$\notin\Sigma\) and let \(\cdot^\$:\Sigma^*\rightarrow(\Sigma\cup\{\$\})^*\) be a morphism defined with _a_<sup>$</sup>=_a_$ for \(a\in\Sigma\). Then, \(\delta_E(X,Y)=\frac{1}{2}\delta_D(X^\$,Y^\$)\) \[Tis15\]. Moreover, if _X_ is represented by a straight line program **G**, then _X_<sup>$</sup> can be represented using a straight-line program of size 2|**G**|+1. This reduction allows computing \(\delta_D\) instead of \(\delta_E\).

**Definition 3.2** (Alignment graph)**.** For two strings _X_ and _Y_ , the alignment graph **G**_<sub>X,Y</sub>_ is a weighted undirected graph with vertex set \(\{v_{x,y}:x\in[0..|X|],y\in[0..|Y|]\}\) and edges:

• \(v_{x,y-1}\leftrightarrow v_{x,y}\) of length 1, for \(x\in[0..|X|]\) and \(y\in[1..|Y|]\);<tbc>

• \(v_{x-1,y}\leftrightarrow v_{x,y}\) of length 1, for \(x\in[1..|X|]\) and \(y\in[0..|Y|]\);<tbc>

• \(v_{x-1,y-1}\leftrightarrow v_{x,y}\) of length 0, for \(x\in[1..|X|]\) and \(y\in[1..|Y|]\) such that _X_\[_x_\]=_Y_\[_y_\].

**Observation 3.3.** _Let d be the metric induced by G<sub>X,Y</sub>. All_ \(x,x'\in[0..|X|]\) _and_ \(y,y'\in[0..|Y|]\)_, satisfy_

\(d(v_{x,y},v_{x^\prime,y^\prime})=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
\delta_D(X(x\dots x'],Y(y\dots y']) & \text{\textit{if}}x\le x'\text{\textit{and}}y\le y', \\
\delta_D(X(x'\dots x],Y(y'\dots y]) & \text{\textit{if}}x'\le x\text{\textit{and}}y'\le y, \\
|x-x'|+|y-y'| & \text{\textit{otherwise}}.
\end{array}\right.\)

For two ranges \([x\dots x']\subseteq[0..|X|]\) and \([y\dots y']\subseteq[0..|Y|]\), the subgraph of _G<sub>X,Y</sub>_ induced by \(\{v_{\bar{x},\bar{y}}:\bar{x}\in[x\dots x'],\bar{y}\in[y\dots y']\}\) is denoted \(G_{X,Y}^{[x\dots x^\prime],[y\dots y^\prime]}\) and called a _block_ in _G<sub>X,Y</sub>_. For a block _B_, we distinguish the _input vertices_ \(\mathrm{in}^B=(v_{x^\prime,y},v_{x^\prime-1,y},\dots,v_{x,y},v_{x,y+1},\dots,v_{x,y^\prime})\) and the _output vertices_ \(\mathrm{out}^B=(v_{x^\prime,y},v_{x^\prime,y+1},\dots,v_{x^\prime,y^\prime},v_{x^\prime-1,y^\prime},\dots,v_{x,y^\prime})\); both sequences consist of \(|B|:=(x'-x)+(y'-y)+1\) vertices. The _DIST<sub>B</sub>_ table is a \(|B|\times|B|\) matrix with entries \(DIST_B[i,j]=d(\mathrm{in}_i^B,\mathrm{out}_j^B)\) for \(i,j\in[1..|B|]\). The _DIST<sub>B</sub>_ table satisfies the Monge property \[Tis15\]: \(DIST_B[i,j]+DIST_B[i',j']\le DIST_B[i,j']+DIST_B[i,j']\) holds for all \(i,i',j,j'\in[1..|B|]\) such that \(i\le i'\) and \(j\le j'\). For two strings \(X,Y\in\Sigma^*\), we also define _DIST<sub>X,Y</sub>_ to be _DIST<sub>B</sub>_ for \(B=G_{X,Y}^{[0..|X|],[0..|Y|]}\). By Observation 3.3, if \(B=G_{X,Y}^{[x\dots x^\prime],[y\dots y^\prime]}\), then \(DIST_B=DIST_{X(x\dots x^\prime],Y(y\dots y^\prime]}\).

### Box decomposition

For two strings \(X,Y\in\Sigma^*\), the _box decomposition_ **B** of the graph _G<sub>X,Y</sub>_ is defined based on decompositions \(X=X_1\circ\cdots\circ X_{p_X}\) and \(Y=Y_1\circ\cdots\circ Y_{p_Y}\) into non-empty fragments, called _phrases_.

Let us define sets \(\{b_0^X,\dots,b_{p_X}^X\}\) and \(\{b_0^Y,\dots,b_{p_Y}^Y\}\) of _phrase boundaries_ in _X_ and _Y_ , respectively, so that the phrases are \(X_i=X(b_{i-1}^X\dots b_i^X]\) for \(i\in[1..p_X]\) and \(Y_j=Y(b_{j-1}^Y\dots b_j^Y]\) for \(j\in[1..p_Y]\). A vertex _v<sub>x,y</sub>_ is a _boundary vertex_ if _x_ is a phrase boundary in _X_ or _y_ is a phrase boundary in _Y_ , and a _grid vertex_ if both _x_ is a phrase boundary in _X_ and _y_ is a phrase boundary in _Y_ . The box decomposition **B** is an indexed family \((B_{i,j})_{i\in[1..p_X],j\in[1..p_Y]}\) of _boxes_ \(B_{i,j}:=G_{X,Y}^{[b_{i-1}^X\dots b_i^X],[b_{j-1}^Y\dots b_j^Y]}\).

## 3.1 Portal-Respecting Walks

Hermelin et al. \[HLLW13\] applied a box decomposition obtained via an analogue of Corollary 3.9 to determine \(\delta_D(X,Y)\) using a dynamic-programming procedure computing \(\delta_D(X[1..x],Y[1..y])\) for all boundary vertices _v<sub>x,y</sub>_. We reduce the number of DP states by considering only a selection **P** of boundary vertices, called _portals_. This allows improving the running time from \(\widetilde{O}(\frac{NM}{\tau})\) to \(\widetilde{O}(|\mathbf{P}|)\), but reduces the search space from the family of all walks \(v_{0,0}\rightsquigarrow v_{x,y}\) to walks that cross box boundaries only at portals. Below, we formally define such portal-respecting walks and provide a construction suitable for approximating \(\delta_D(X,Y)\).

**Definition 3.4.** Let **B** be a box decomposition of _G<sub>X,Y</sub>_ and let **P** be a set _portals_ (selected boundary vertices). We say that a walk _W_ is a _portal-respecting_ (_i,j)-walk_ if _W_ is a concatenation of walks \(W'\) and \(W''\) such that:

• \(W''\) starts at an input portal of _B<sub>i,j</sub>_ and is entirely contained within _B<sub>i,j</sub>_, and<tbc>

• \(W'\) is the empty walk at _v_<sub>0,0</sub>, a portal-respecting (_i_-1_,j_)-walk, or a portal-respecting (_i,j_-1)-walk.

Let us fix a box decomposition **B** of _G<sub>X,Y</sub>_, and a set of portals **P**. For a box \(B_{i,j}\in\mathbf{B}\), let \(\mathbf{P}_{i,j}=\mathbf{P}\cap\mathrm{out}^{B_{i,j}}\) denote the output portals of _B<sub>i,j</sub>_. Moreover, for a vertex \(v_{x,y}\in B_{i,j}\), we denote \(d_{x,y}=d(v_{0,0},v_{x,y})=\delta_D(X[1..x],Y[1..y])\) and let \(D_{x,y}^{i,j}\) be the minimum length of a portal-preserving (_i,j_)-walk ending at _v<sub>x,y</sub>_.

**Lemma 3.5.** _Given a set of portals_ **P** _for a box decomposition_ **B** _of G<sub>X,Y</sub>, the length of the shortest portal-respecting_ (_p<sub>X</sub>,p<sub>Y</sub>)-walk ending at v_<sub>|_X_|,|_Y_|</sub> _can be computed in_ \(\widetilde{O}(|\mathbf{P}|)\) _time provided_ \(\widetilde{O}(1)\)_-time random access to the DIST matrices of all the boxes of_ **B**.

_Proof._ For each box \(B_{i,j}\in\mathbf{B}\), our algorithm computes \(D_{x,y}^{i,j}\) for all vertices \(v_{x,y}\in\mathbf{P}_{i,j}\). For this, the boxes _B<sub>i,j</sub>_ containing any output portal are processed in the order of non-decreasing values _i+j_.

If (_i,j_)=(1,1), then Definition 3.4 and Observation 3.3 yield \(D_{x,y}^{1,1}=d(v_{0,0},v_{x,y})\), and this value can be retrieved from the _DIST_<sub>_B_<sub>1,1</sub></sub> matrix in \(\widetilde{O}(1)\) time. Thus, we henceforth assume \((i,j)\neq(1,1)\).

Consider a portal-respecting (_i,j_)-walk _W_ to a vertex \(v_{x,y}\in\mathrm{out}^{B_{i,j}}\). By Definition 3.4, _W_ is a concatenation of two walks \(W'\) and \(W''\) such that \(W''\) starts at a vertex \(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\in\mathbf{P}\cap\mathrm{in}^{B_{i,j}}\) and is entirely contained within _B<sub>i,j</sub>_, whereas \(W'\) is a portal-respecting (_i,j_-1)-walk to \(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\) or a portal respecting (_i_-1_,j_)-walk to \(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\). Observe that, for a fixed portal \(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\in\mathbf{P}\cap\mathrm{in}^{B_{i,j}}\), the lengths of \(W'\) and \(W''\) can be optimized independently. Consequently, by Observation 3.3,

\(D_{x,y}^{i,j}=\mathrm{max}\left(\mathrm{max}_{v_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\in\mathbf{P}_{i-1,j}\cap\mathrm{in}^{B_{i,j}}}\left\{D_{x^\prime,y^\prime}^{i-1,j}+d(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime},v_{x,y})\right\},\mathrm{max}_{v_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\in\mathbf{P}_{i,j-1}\cap\mathrm{in}^{B_{i,j}}}\left\{D_{x^\prime,y^\prime}^{i,j-1}+d(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime},v_{x,y})\right\}\right).\)

A matrix (indexed by \(v_{x,y}\in\mathbf{P}_{i,j}\) and all vertices \(\mathbf{P}_{i-1,j}\cap\mathrm{in}^{B_{i,j}}\)) containing the values \(D_{x^\prime,y^\prime}^{i-1,j}+d(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime},v_{x,y})\) can be obtained from a submatrix of the _DIST<sub>B<sub>i,j</sub></sub>_ matrix by adding \(D_{x^\prime,y^\prime}^{i-1,j}\) to all entries in the column of \(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\). These modifications preserve the Monge property, so the resulting matrix is a Monge matrix with \(\widetilde{O}(1)\)-time random access. Consequently, the SMAWK algorithm \[AKM<sup>+</sup>87\] allows computing row-minima, i.e., the values \(\mathrm{max}_{v_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\in\mathbf{P}_{i-1,j}\cap\mathrm{in}^{B_{i,j}}}\left\{D_{x^\prime,y^\prime}^{i-1,j}+d(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime},v_{x,y})\right\}\). A symmetric procedure allows computing the values \(\mathrm{max}_{v_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\in\mathbf{P}_{i,j-1}\cap\mathrm{in}^{B_{i,j}}}\left\{D_{x^\prime,y^\prime}^{i,j-1}+d(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime},v_{x,y})\right\}\), which lets us derive the costs \(D_{x,y}^{i,j}\) for all the vertices \(v_{x,y}\in\mathbf{P}_{i,j}\). The SMAWK algorithm takes nearly linear time with respect to the sum of matrix dimensions, so the overall time complexity is \(\widetilde{O}(|\mathbf{P}\cap B_{i,j}|)\).

Each vertex belongs to at most four boxes, so the overall running time is \(\widetilde{O}(|\mathbf{P}|)\).

**Lemma 3.6.** _Let_ **B** _be a box decomposition of the graph G<sub>X,Y</sub> for_ \(X,Y\in\Sigma^+\) _and let_ \(\alpha>0\) _be a real number. Suppose that_ **P** _consists of all the grid vertices and all the boundary vertices v<sub>x,y</sub> of_ **B** _satisfying_ \(|x-y|=\lfloor(1+\alpha)^r\rfloor\) _for some integer r. Then, every vertex_ \(v_{x,y}\in B_{i,j}\) _satisfies_ \(D_{x,y}^{i,j}\le(1+2\alpha)^{i+j}d_{x,y}\).

_Proof._ We proceed by induction on _i+j_. The base case is trivially satisfied due to \(D_{x,y}^{1,1}=d_{x,y}\) for \(v_{x,y}\in B_{1,1}\). We henceforth fix \(v_{x,y}\in B_{i,j}\) with \((i,j)\neq(1,1)\). By Observation 3.3, there is a shortest path from _v_<sub>0,0</sub> to _v<sub>x,y</sub>_ contained within _G_<sub>_X_\[1_..x_\]_,Y_\[1_..y_\]</sub>. Let \(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\) be the first vertex of _B<sub>i,j</sub>_ on this path. Observe that \(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\in\mathrm{in}^{B_{i,j}}\) and \(d_{x,y}=d_{x^\prime,y^\prime}+d(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime},v_{x,y})\). By symmetry, we may assume without loss of generality that \(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\in\mathrm{out}^{B_{i-1,j}}\).

Let us choose \(v_{x^\prime,y^{\prime\prime}}\in\mathbf{P}_{i-1,j}\cap\mathrm{out}^{B_{i-1,j}}\) as close as possible to \(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\). Since grid vertices are portals, such \(v_{x^\prime,y^{\prime\prime}}\) exists. Moreover, by the choice of the remaining portals, \(d(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime},v_{x^\prime,y^{\prime\prime}})\le\alpha|x'-y'|\le\alpha d_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\). Let us construct a portal-respecting (_i,j_)-walk to _v<sub>x,y</sub>_ by concatenating a shortest portal-respecting (_i_-1_,j_)-walk to \(v_{x^\prime,y^{\prime\prime}}\) and a shortest path from \(v_{x^\prime,y^{\prime\prime}}\) to _v<sub>x,y</sub>_ (by Observation 3.3, we may assume that this path is contained in _B<sub>i,j</sub>_). This proves \(D_{x,y}^{i,j}\le D_{x,y}^{i-1,j}+d(v_{x^\prime,y^{\prime\prime}},v_{x,y})\). The inductive assumption further yields \(D_{x,y}^{i-1,j}\le(1+2\alpha)^{i+j-3}d_{x^\prime,y^{\prime\prime}}\), and thus \(D_{x,y}^{i,j}\le(1+2\alpha)^{i+j-3}d_{x^\prime,y^{\prime\prime}}+d(v_{x^\prime,y^{\prime\prime}},v_{x,y})\le(1+2\alpha)^{i+j-3}(d_{x^\prime,y^\prime}+d(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime},v_{x^\prime,y^{\prime\prime}}))+d(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime},v_{x^\prime,y^{\prime\prime}})+d_{x,y}-d_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\le(1+2\alpha)^{i+j-3}(d_{x^\prime,y^\prime}+\alpha d_{x^\prime,y^\prime})+\alpha d_{x^\prime,y^\prime}+d_{x,y}-d_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\le(1+2\alpha)^{i+j-2}d_{x,y}\).

## 3.2 A Grammar-Based Box Decomposition

Hermelin et al. \[HLLW13\] presented an algorithm that, given two grammar-compressed strings \(X,Y\in\Sigma^+\) and an integer parameter \(\tau\), constructs a box decomposition **B** of _G<sub>X,Y</sub>_ with \(p_X=O(\lceil\frac{1}{\tau}|X|\rceil)\) and \(p_Y=O(\lceil\frac{1}{\tau}|Y|\rceil)\), along with an oracle providing random access to the _DIST<sub>B<sub>i,j</sub></sub>_ matrices of all the boxes _B<sub>i,j</sub>_. However, their construction costs \(\Omega(|X|+|Y|)\) time, which is prohibitive in most of our applications. In this section, we achieve the same goal avoiding the linear dependency on the lengths of _X_ and _Y_ . The bottleneck of \[HLLW13\] is constructing appropriate decompositions of _X_ and _Y_ into phrases. In the following lemma, we implement an analogous step more efficiently by building a grammar-compressed representation of the sequence of phrases, with each phrase represented by a symbol in an auxiliary grammar.

**Lemma 3.7.** _Given a straight-line program_ **G** _generating a string X and an integer_ \(\tau\ge 1\)_, in O_(|**G**|) _time one can construct straight-line programs_ **G**<sup>+</sup> _and_ **G**_<sup>P</sup> of size O_(|**G**|) _such that:_

• _the terminal symbols of_ **G**_<sup>P</sup> are the symbols A of_ **G**<sup>+</sup> _satisfying_ \(|A|\le\tau\),<tbc>

• **G**_<sup>P</sup> generates a string P such that_ exp<sub>**G**<sup>+</sup></sub>(_P_)=_X and_ \(|P|\le\big\lceil\frac{3}{\tau}|X|\big\rceil\).

_Proof._ If \(\tau\ge|X|\), then we simply set **G**<sup>+</sup>=**G** and set **G**_<sup>P</sup>_ to be a grammar with no non-terminals whose starting symbol is the starting symbol of **G**; this construction clearly satisfies the required conditions.

We henceforth assume that \(\tau<|X|\). The grammar **G**<sup>+</sup> is constructed by adding new non-terminals to **G**. As for **G**_<sup>P</sup>_, we include as terminals all symbols _A_ of **G**<sup>+</sup> with \(|A|\le\tau\), and we add further symbols as non-terminals. For every symbol _A_ of **G** with \(|A|>\tau\), we introduce three new non-terminals:

• _L(A_) and _R(A_) to **G**<sup>+</sup>, satisfying \(|L(A)|\le\tau\) and \(|R(A)|\le\tau\),<tbc>

• _M(A_) to **G**_<sup>P</sup>_.

The productions for _L(A_), _R(A_), and _M(A_) are determined based on the production \(A\rightarrow B_LB_R\):

1. If \(|B_L|\le\tau\) and \(|B_R|\le\tau\), then \(M(A)\rightarrow\gamma\), \(L(A)\rightarrow B_L\), and \(R(A)\rightarrow B_R\).<tbc>

2. If \(|B_L|>\tau\) and \(|B_R|>\tau\), then \(M(A)\rightarrow M(B_L)R(B_L)L(B_R)M(B_R)\), \(L(A)\rightarrow L(B_L)\), and \(R(A)\rightarrow R(B_R)\).<tbc>

3. If \(|B_L|>\tau\) and \(|B_R|\le\tau\), then \(L(A)\rightarrow L(B_L)\) and:<tbc>

(a) \(R(A)\rightarrow R(B_L)B_R\) and \(M(A)\rightarrow M(B_L)\) if \(|R(B_L)|+|B_R|\le\tau\),<tbc>

(b) \(R(A)\rightarrow B_R\) and \(M(A)\rightarrow M(B_L)R(B_L)\) otherwise.<tbc>

4. If \(|B_L|\le\tau\) and \(|B_R|>\tau\), then \(R(A)\rightarrow R(B_R)\) and:<tbc>

(a) \(L(A)\rightarrow B_LL(B_R)\) and \(M(A)\rightarrow M(B_R)\) if \(|B_L|+|L(B_R)|\le\tau\),<tbc>

(b) \(L(A)\rightarrow B_L\) and \(M(A)\rightarrow L(B_R)M(B_R)\) otherwise.

Additionally, for the starting symbol _S_ of **G**, we add a starting symbol \(S^P\rightarrow L(S)M(S)R(S)\) to **G**_<sup>P</sup>_.

A simple inductive argument shows that every symbol _A_ of **G** with \(|A|>\tau\) satisfies

\(\mathrm{exp}_\mathbf{G}(A)=\mathrm{exp}_{\mathbf{G}^+}(L(A)\circ\mathrm{exp}_{\mathbf{G}^P}(M(A))\circ R(A)).\)

In particular, _P_=exp<sub>**G**_<sup>P</sup>_</sub>(_S<sup>P</sup>_) satisfies exp<sub>**G**<sup>+</sup></sub>(_P_)=exp<sub>**G**</sub>(_S_)=_X_.

It remains to prove that \(|P|<\frac{3}{\tau}|X|\). For this, we inductively show that every symbol _A_ of **G** with \(|A|>\tau\) satisfies \(|L(A)|+|R(A)|+\tau(|M(A)|+2)<3|A|\). To prove this claim, we analyze the cases based on the production \(A\rightarrow B_LB_R\).

1. If \(|B_L|\le\tau\) and \(|B_R|\le\tau\), then<tbc>

<tbc>\(|L(A)|+|R(A)|+\tau(|M(A)|+2)=|A|+2\tau<3|A|.\)<tbc>

2. If \(|B_L|>\tau\) and \(|B_R|>\tau\), then<tbc>

<tbc>\(|L(A)|+|R(A)|+\tau(|M(A)|+2)=|L(B_L)|+|R(B_R)|+\tau(|M(B_L)|+2+|M(B_R)|+2)<|L(B_L)|+|R(B_L)|+\tau(|M(B_L)|+2)+|L(B_R)|+\tau(|M(B_R)|+2)<3|B_L|+3|B_R|=3|A|.\)<tbc>

3. If \(|B_L|>\tau\), \(|B_R|\le\tau\), then<tbc>

• If \(|R(B_L)|+|B_R|\le\tau\), then<tbc>

<tbc>\(|L(A)|+|R(A)|+\tau(|M(A)|+2)=|L(B_L)|+|R(B_L)|+|B_R|+\tau(|M(B_L)|+2)<3|B_L|+|B_R|<3|A|.\)<tbc>

• Otherwise,<tbc>

<tbc>\(|L(A)|+|R(A)|+\tau(|M(A)|+2)=|L(B_L)|+|B_R|+\tau(|M(B_L)|+3)<|L(B_L)|+|B_R|+\tau(|M(B_L)|+2)+|R(B_L)|+|B_R|<3|B_L|+2|B_R|<3|A|.\)<tbc>

4. The case involving \(|B_L|\le\tau\) and \(|B_R|>\tau\) is symmetric to the previous one.

In particular, this claim holds for _A=S_, so \(|S^P|=|M(S)|+2<\frac{1}{\tau}(3|S|-|L(S)|-|R(S)|)<\frac{3}{\tau}|S|=\frac{3}{\tau}|X|\).

As for constructing the _DIST_ matrices, we use the original implementation from \[HLLW13\].

**Lemma 3.8** (\[HLLW13, Section 5\])**.** _Given straight-line programs_ **G**_<sub>X</sub> and_ **G**_<sub>Y</sub> and an integer_ \(\tau\ge 1\)_, in_ \(\widetilde{O}(|\mathbf{G}_X||\mathbf{G}_Y|\tau)\) _time one can construct a data structure that provides_ \(\widetilde{O}(1)\)_-time random access to the DIST_<sub>exp(_A<sub>X</sub>),_exp(_A<sub>Y</sub>_)</sub> _matrices for all symbols A<sub>X</sub> of_ **G**_<sub>X</sub> and A<sub>Y</sub> of_ **G**_<sub>Y</sub> satisfying_ \(|A_X|\le\tau\) _and_ \(|A_Y|\le\tau\).

Combining Lemmas 3.7 and 3.8, we complete our construction.

**Corollary 3.9.** _Given a straight-line program_ **G**_<sub>X</sub> of size n generating a string X of length N\>_0_, a straight-line program_ **G**_<sub>Y</sub> of size m generating a string Y of length M\>_0_, and an integer_ \(\tau\in[1..N+M]\)_, one can in_ \(\widetilde{O}(\frac{N+M}{\tau}+nm\tau)\) _time construct a box decomposition_ \(\mathbf{B}=(B_{i,j})_{i\in[1..p_X],j\in[1..p_Y]}\) _of G<sub>X,Y</sub> with_ \(p_X=O(\lceil\frac{N}{\tau}\rceil)\) _and_ \(p_Y=O(\lceil\frac{M}{\tau}\rceil)\)_, along with an oracle providing_ \(\widetilde{O}(1)\)_-time random access to the DIST<sub>B<sub>i,j</sub></sub> matrices._

_Proof._ First, we use Lemma 3.7 to obtain grammars \(\mathbf{G}_X^+\) and \(\mathbf{G}_X^P\). The string _P<sub>X</sub>_ represented by \(\mathbf{G}_X^P\) satisfies \(X=\mathrm{exp}_{\mathbf{G}_X^+}(P_X)\), so it can be interpreted as a decomposition of _X_ into _p<sub>X</sub>_:=|_P<sub>X</sub>_| phrases, with the _i_th phrase _X<sub>i</sub>_ being an occurrence of \(\mathrm{exp}_{\mathbf{G}_X^+}(P_X[i])\). The decomposition of _Y_ is obtained in the same way based on grammars \(\mathbf{G}_Y^+\) and \(\mathbf{G}_Y^P\) constructed for _Y_ .

The box decomposition **B** is based on these decompositions of _X_ and _Y_ . Note that each box _B<sub>i,j</sub>_ satisfies

\(DIST_{B_{i,j}}=DIST_{\mathrm{exp}_{\mathbf{G}_X^+}(P_X[i]),\mathrm{exp}_{\mathbf{G}_Y^+}(P_Y[j])}.\)

Due to \(|P_X[i]|\le\tau\) and \(|P_Y[j]|\le\tau\), Lemma 3.8 applied to \(\mathbf{G}_X^+\) and \(\mathbf{G}_Y^+\) provides \(\widetilde{O}(1)\)-time oracle access to all these matrices. Storing _P<sub>X</sub>_ and _P<sub>Y</sub>_, we can point to _DIST<sub>B<sub>i,j</sub></sub>_ in _O_(1) time given _i,j_.

## 3.3 Algorithm

**Proposition 3.10.** _Given a straight-line program_ **G**_<sub>X</sub> of size n generating a string X of length N\>_0_, a straight-line program_ **G**_<sub>Y</sub> of size m generating a string Y of length M\>_0_, and a parameter_ \(\epsilon\in(0,1]\)_, a_ \((1+\epsilon)\)_-approximation of_ \(\delta_D(X,Y)\) _can be computed in_ \(\widetilde{O}\left((nm(N+M))^{2/3}\epsilon^{-1/3}\right)\) _time._

_Proof._ The algorithm uses Corollary 3.9 and Lemma 3.5 with the set of portals **P** defined as in Lemma 3.6, where \(\alpha=\Omega(\frac{\epsilon}{p_X+p_Y-2})=\Omega(\frac{\epsilon\tau}{N+M})\) is chosen so that \((1+2\alpha)^{p_X+p_Y-2}=1+\epsilon\). Lemma 3.6 guar antes that the resulting value is a \((1+\epsilon)\)-approximation of \(\delta_D(X,Y)\). The number of portals is \(O\left(\frac{NM}{\tau^2}+\frac{N}{\tau}\mathrm{log}_{1+\alpha} M+\frac{M}{\tau}\mathrm{log}_{1+\alpha} N\right)=\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{(N+M)^2}{\epsilon\tau^2}\right)\), so the overall running time is \(\widetilde{O}\left(nm\tau+\frac{(N+M)^2}{\epsilon\tau^2}\right)\). Optimizing \(\tau\in[1..N+M]\), we get \(\widetilde{O}(nm+\epsilon^{-1}+(nm(N+M))^{2/3}\epsilon^{-1/3})\) time. If the first term dominates, then \(nm\ge(nm(N+M))^{2/3}\epsilon^{-1/3}\ge(N+M)^2\epsilon^{-1}\). However, \(O(NM)=O((N+M)^2\epsilon^{-1})\) time is enough to compute \(\delta_D(X,Y)\) exactly without compression. If the second term dominates, then \(\epsilon^{-1}\ge(nm(N+M))^{2/3}\epsilon^{-1/3}\ge nm(N+M)\). However, \(\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{nm}(N+M))=\widetilde{O}(nm(N+M))\) time is enough to compute \(\delta_D(X,Y)\) exactly using Proposition 3.13 with _D=N+M_.

## 3.4 Exact Output-Sensitive Algorithm

In this section we prove Theorem 3.11:

**Theorem 3.11.** _Given a straight-line program_ **G**_<sub>X</sub> of size n generating a string X of length N\>_0 _and a straight-line program_ **G**_<sub>Y</sub> of size m generating a string Y of length M\>_0_, the edit distance_ \(\delta_E(X,Y)\) _can be computed in_ \(\widetilde{O}\left(\sqrt{(1+\delta_E(X,Y))nm(N+M)}\right)\) _time._

The algorithm behind Theorem 3.11 reduces the problem to a decision version (asking whether \(\delta_E(X,Y)\le D\) for a threshold _D_) and then uses the same scheme with all boundary vertices (_x,y_) satisfying \(|x-y|\le D\) selected as portals.

**Lemma 3.12.** _Let_ **B** _be a box decomposition of the graph G<sub>X,Y</sub> for_ \(X,Y\in\Sigma^+\) _and let_ \(D\ge 0\) _be an integer. Suppose that_ **P** _consists of all the boundary vertices v<sub>x,y</sub> of_ **B** _satisfying_ \(|x-y|\le D\)_. Then, every vertex_ \(v_{x,y}\in B_{i,j}\) _with_ \(d_{x,y}\le D\) _satisfies_ \(D_{x,y}^{i,j}=d_{x,y}\).

_Proof._ We proceed by induction on _i+j_. The base case is trivially satisfied due to \(D_{x,y}^{1,1}=d_{x,y}\) for \(v_{x,y}\in B_{1,1}\). We henceforth fix \(v_{x,y}\in B_{i,j}\) with \((i,j)\neq(1,1)\) and \(d_{x,y}\le D\). By Observation 3.3, there is a shortest path from _v_<sub>0,0</sub> to _v<sub>x,y</sub>_ contained within _G_<sub>_X_\[1_..x_\]_,Y_\[1_..y_\]</sub>. Let \(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\) be the first vertex on this path that belongs to _B<sub>i,j</sub>_. Observe that \(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\in\mathrm{in}^{B_{i,j}}\) and \(d_{x,y}=d_{x^\prime,y^\prime}+d(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime},v_{x,y})\). Consequently, \(|x'-y'|\le d_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\le d_{x,y}\le D\), so \(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\in\mathbf{P}_{i-1,j}\cup\mathbf{P}_{i,j-1}\). By symmetry, we may assume without loss of generality that \(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\in\mathbf{P}_{i-1,j}\).

Let us construct a portal-respecting (_i,j_)-walk to _v<sub>x,y</sub>_ by concatenating a shortest portal-respecting (_i_-1_,j_)-walk to \(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\) and a shortest path from \(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\) to _v<sub>x,y</sub>_ (by Observation 3.3 applied to \(G_{X(x^\prime..x],Y(y^\prime..y]}\),<tbc>

<tbc>we may assume that this path is contained in _B<sub>i,j</sub>_). This proves \(D_{x,y}^{i,j}\le D_{x^\prime,y^\prime}^{i-1,j}+d(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime},v_{x,y})=D_{x,y}^{i,j}\le D_{x^\prime,y^\prime}^{i-1,j}+d_{x,y}-d_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\). The inductive assumption yields \(D_{x^\prime,y^\prime}^{i-1,j}=d_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\), and thus \(D_{x,y}^{i,j}\le d_{x,y}\) holds as claimed.

**Proposition 3.13.** _Given a straight-line program_ **G**_<sub>X</sub> of size n generating a string X of length N\>_0_, a straight-line program_ **G**_<sub>Y</sub> of size m generating a string Y of length M\>_0_, and an integer_ \(D\in[1..N+M]\)_, one can in_ \(\widetilde{O}\left(\sqrt{nmD(N+M)}\right)\) _time compute_ \(\delta_D(X,Y)\) _or certify that_ \(\delta_D(X,Y)>D\).

_Proof._ The algorithm uses Corollary 3.9 and Lemma 3.5 with the set of portals **P** defined as in Lemma 3.12. The latter lemma guarantees that the resulting value is \(\delta_D(X,Y)\) provided that \(\delta_D(X,Y)\le D\). Otherwise, the resulting value exceeds _D_, certifying that \(\delta_D(X,Y)>D\).

The number of portals is \(O(D\cdot\frac{N+M}{\tau})\), so the overall running time is \(\widetilde{O}(nm\tau+D\cdot\frac{N+M}{\tau})\). Optimizing \(\tau\in[1..N+M]\), we get \(\widetilde{O}(nm+D+\sqrt{nmD(N+M)})\) time. Since \(D\le N+M\), the second term is dominated by the third one. If the first term dominates, then _nm\>D(N+M_), and thus \(\sqrt{nmD(N+M)}\ge D(N+M)\). However, \(\widetilde{O}(N+M+D^2)=\widetilde{O}(D(N+M))\) time suffices solve the problem for uncompressed strings \[LV88\].

Theorem 3.11 follows through exponential search and the reduction from \(\delta_E\) to \(\delta_D\).

## 3.5 LCS Approximation

In this section we prove Theorem 3.14:

**Theorem 3.14.** _Given a straight-line program_ **G**_<sub>X</sub> of size n generating a string X of length N\>_0_, a straight-line program_ **G**_<sub>Y</sub> of size m generating a string Y of length M\>_0_, and a parameter_ \(\epsilon\in(0,1]\)_, a_ \((1+\epsilon)\)_-approximation of_ LCS(_X,Y_) _can be computed in_ \(\widetilde{O}\left((nm(N+M))^{2/3}\epsilon^{-1/3}\right)\) _time._

The algorithm behind Theorem 3.14 is essentially the same as that of Theorem 3.1, and this is why the running times coincide. The main difference is that the output portals of the box _B<sub>i,j</sub>_ are chosen _adaptively_ while the dynamic-programming algorithm processes _B<sub>i,j</sub>_.

As for LCS approximation, our choice of portals is _adaptive_. For a box \(B_{i,j}\in\mathbf{B}\), let \(\mathbf{P}_{i,j}=\mathbf{P}\cap\mathrm{out}^{B_{i,j}}\). Observe that the value \(D_{x,y}^{i,j}\) for \(v_{x,y}\in B_{i,j}\) depends only on \(\mathbf{P}_{i^\prime,j^\prime}\) with \(i'+j'<i+j\). Hence, except for the grid vertices (all included in **P**), we may select the portals **P**_<sub>i,j</sub>_ based on the values \(D_{x,y}^{i,j}\) for \(v_{x,y}\in\mathrm{out}^{B_{i,j}}\).

For \(v_{x,y}\in B_{i,j}\), let \(\ell_{x,y}=\frac{1}{2}(|X|+|Y|-d_{x,y})=\mathrm{LCS}(X[1..x],Y[1..y])\) and \(L_{x,y}^{i,j}=\frac{1}{2}(|X|+|Y|-D_{x,y}^{i,j})\).

**Lemma 3.15.** _Let_ **B** _be a box decomposition of the graph G<sub>X,Y</sub> for_ \(X,Y\in\Sigma^+\) _and let_ \(\alpha>0\) _be a real number. Suppose that_ **P** _consists of all the grid vertices and, for each box_ \(B_{i,j}\in\mathbf{B}\)_, all vertices_ \(v_{x,y}\in\mathrm{out}^{B_{i,j}}\) _such that:_

• \(v_{x-1,y}\in\mathrm{out}^{B_{i,j}}\) _and_ \(\lfloor\mathrm{log}_{1+\alpha} L_{x,y}^{i,j}\rfloor>\lfloor\mathrm{log}_{1+\alpha} L_{x-1,y}^{i,j}\rfloor\)_, or_<tbc>

• \(v_{x,y-1}\in\mathrm{out}^{B_{i,j}}\) _and_ \(\lfloor\mathrm{log}_{1+\alpha} L_{x,y}^{i,j}\rfloor>\lfloor\mathrm{log}_{1+\alpha} L_{x,y-1}^{i,j}\rfloor\).

_Then, for each vertex_ \(v_{x,y}\in B_{i,j}\)_, we have_ \(L_{x,y}^{i,j}\ge(1+\alpha)^{2-i-j}\ell_{x,y}\).

_Proof._ We proceed by induction on _i+j_. The base case is trivially satisfied due to \(L_{x,y}^{1,1}=\ell_{x,y}\) for \(v_{x,y}\in B_{1,1}\). Thus, we henceforth fix a vertex \(v_{x,y}\in B_{i,j}\) with \((i,j)\neq(1,1)\). By Observation 3.3, there is a shortest path from _v_<sub>0,0</sub> to _v<sub>x,y</sub>_ contained within _G_<sub>_X_\[1_..x_\]_,Y_\[1_..y_\]</sub>. Let \(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\) be the first vertex on this path that belong to _B<sub>i,j</sub>_. Observe that \(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\in\mathrm{in}^{B_{i,j}}\) and \(\ell_{x,y}=\ell_{x^\prime,y^\prime}+\mathrm{LCS}(X(x'..x],Y(y'..y])\). By symmetry, we may assume without loss of generality that \(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\in\mathrm{out}^{B_{i-1,j}}\).

Consider the largest value \(y''\in[1..y']\) such that \(v_{x^\prime,y^{\prime\prime}}\in\mathbf{P}_{i-1,j}\). Since grid vertices are portals, such \(v_{x^\prime,y^{\prime\prime}}\) exits. Moreover, by the choice of the remaining portals, \(L_{x^\prime,y^\prime}^{i-1,j}\le(1+\alpha)L_{x^\prime,y^{\prime\prime}}^{i-1,j}\). Let us construct a portal-respecting (_i,j_) walk to _v<sub>x,y</sub>_ by concatenating a shortest portal-respecting (_i_-1_,j_)-walk to \(v_{x^\prime,y^{\prime\prime}}\) and a shortest path from \(v_{x^\prime,y^{\prime\prime}}\) to _v<sub>x,y</sub>_ (by Observation 3.3, we may assume that this path is contained _B<sub>i,j</sub>_). This proves that \(D_{x,y}^{i,j}\le D_{x^\prime,y^{\prime\prime}}^{i-1,j}+d(v_{x^\prime,y^{\prime\prime}},v_{x,y})\le D_{x^\prime,y^{\prime\prime}}^{i-1,j}+y'-y''+d(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime},v_{x,y})\), i.e., \(L_{x,y}^{i,j}\ge L_{x^\prime,y^{\prime\prime}}^{i-1,j}+\mathrm{LCS}(X(x'..x],Y(y'..y])\ge(1+\alpha)^{-1}L_{x^\prime,y^\prime}^{i-1,j}+\ell_{x,y}-\ell_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\). The inductive assumption further yields \(L_{x^\prime,y^\prime}^{i-1,j}\ge(1+\alpha)^{3-i-j}\ell_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\), and thus \(L_{x,y}^{i,j}\ge(1+\alpha)^{2-i-j}\ell_{x^\prime,y^\prime}+\ell_{x,y}-\ell_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\ge(1+\alpha)^{2-i-j}\ell_{x,y}\) holds as claimed.

**Lemma 3.16.** _Given_ \(\widetilde{O}(1)\)_-time random access to the DIST<sub>B<sub>i,j</sub></sub> matrix, the values_ \(D_{x^\prime,y^\prime}^{i-1,j}\) _for all vertices_ \(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\in\mathbf{P}_{i-1,j}\) _(if i\>_1_), and the values_ \(D_{x^\prime,y^\prime}^{i,j-1}\) _for all vertices_ \(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\in\mathbf{P}_{i,j-1}\) _(if j\>_1_), the values_ \(D_{x,y}^{i,j}\) _for any q_ query vertices \(v_{x,y}\in\mathrm{out}^{B_{i,j}}\) _can be computed in_ \(\widetilde{O}(q+|\mathbf{P}\cap\mathrm{in}^{B_{i,j}}|)\) _time._

_Proof._ If (_i,j_)=(1,1), then Definition 3.4 and Observation 3.3 yield \(D_{x,y}^{1,1}=d(v_{0,0},v_{x,y})\), and this value can be retrieved from the _DIST_<sub>_B_<sub>1,1</sub></sub> matrix in \(\widetilde{O}(1)\) time. Thus, we henceforth assume \((i,j)\neq(1,1)\).

Consider a portal-respecting (_i,j_)-walk _W_ to a vertex \(v_{x,y}\in\mathrm{out}^{B_{i,j}}\). By Definition 3.4, _W_ is a concatenation of two walks \(W'\) and \(W''\) such that \(W''\) starts at a vertex \(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\in\mathbf{P}\cap\mathrm{in}^{B_{i,j}}\) and is entirely contained within _B<sub>i,j</sub>_, whereas \(W'\) is a portal-respecting (_i,j_-1)-walk to \(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\) or a portal respecting (_i_-1_,j_)-walk to \(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\). Observe that, for a fixed portal \(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\in\mathbf{P}\cap\mathrm{in}^{B_{i,j}}\), the lengths of \(W'\) and \(W''\) can be optimized independently. Consequently, by Observation 3.3,

\(D_{x,y}^{i,j}=\mathrm{max}\left(\mathrm{max}_{v_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\in\mathbf{P}_{i-1,j}\cap\mathrm{in}^{B_{i,j}}}\left\{D_{x^\prime,y^\prime}^{i-1,j}+d(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime},v_{x,y})\right\},\mathrm{max}_{v_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\in\mathbf{P}_{i,j-1}\cap\mathrm{in}^{B_{i,j}}}\left\{D_{x^\prime,y^\prime}^{i,j-1}+d(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime},v_{x,y})\right\}\right).\)

A matrix (indexed by the query vertices \(v_{x,y}\in\mathrm{out}^{B_{i,j}}\) and all vertices \(\mathbf{P}_{i-1,j}\cap\mathrm{in}^{B_{i,j}}\)) containing the values \(D_{x^\prime,y^\prime}^{i-1,j}+d(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime},v_{x,y})\) can be obtained from a submatrix of the _DIST<sub>B<sub>i,j</sub></sub>_ matrix by adding \(D_{x^\prime,y^\prime}^{i-1,j}\) to all entries in the column of \(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\). These modifications preserve the Monge property, so the resulting matrix is a Monge matrix with \(\widetilde{O}(1)\)-time random access. Consequently, the SMAWK algorithm \[AKM<sup>+</sup>87\] allows computing row-minima, i.e., the values \(\mathrm{max}_{v_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\in\mathbf{P}_{i-1,j}\cap\mathrm{in}^{B_{i,j}}}\left\{D_{x^\prime,y^\prime}^{i-1,j}+d(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime},v_{x,y})\right\}\). A symmetric procedure allows computing the values \(\mathrm{max}_{v_{x^\prime,y^\prime}\in\mathbf{P}_{i,j-1}\cap\mathrm{in}^{B_{i,j}}}\left\{D_{x^\prime,y^\prime}^{i,j-1}+d(v_{x^\prime,y^\prime},v_{x,y})\right\}\), which lets us derive the costs \(D_{x,y}^{i,j}\) for all the query vertices \(v_{x,y}\in\mathrm{out}^{B_{i,j}}\). The SMAWK algorithm takes nearly linear time with respect to the sum of matrix dimensions, so the overall time complexity is \(\widetilde{O}(q+|\mathbf{P}\cap\mathrm{in}^{B_{i,j}}|)\).

**Lemma 3.17.** _Given a box decomposition_ **B** _of G<sub>X,Y</sub>, a parameter_ \(\epsilon\in(0,1]\)_, and_ \(\widetilde{O}(1)\)_-time random access to the DIST matrices of all the boxes of_ **B**_, a_ \((1+\epsilon)\)_-approximation of_ LCS(_X,Y_) _can be computed in_ \(\widetilde{O}(\epsilon^{-1}(p_X+p_Y)^2)\) _time._

_Proof._ Let us choose \(\alpha=\Omega(\frac{\epsilon}{p_X+p_Y-2})\) so that \((1+\alpha)^{p_X+p_Y-2}=1+\epsilon\). We process boxes \(B_{i,j}\in\mathbf{B}\) in the order of non-decreasing values _i+j_, constructing the output portals _P<sub>i,j</sub>_ according to Lemma 3.15 and computing the values \(L_{x,y}^{i,j}\) for all \(v_{x,y}\in\mathbf{P}_{i,j}\). By Lemma 3.15, the value \(L_{|X|,|Y|}^{p_X,p_Y}\) is guaranteed to be a \((1+\epsilon)\)-approximation of LCS(_X,Y_).

The ordering of boxes lets us compute the values \(L_{x,y}^{i,j}\) for any _q_ vertices \(v\in\mathrm{out}^{B_{i,j}}\) in \(\widetilde{O}(q+|\mathbf{P}\cap\mathrm{in}^{B_{i,j}}|)\) time. By symmetry, we may focus without loss of generality on the right boundary of _B<sub>i,j</sub>_, i.e., vertices _v<sub>x,y</sub>_ with \(x=b_i^X\) and \(y\in[b_{j-1}^Y\dots b_j^Y]\). Note that the corresponding values \(L_{x,y}^{i,j}\) are non-decreasing: \(D_{x,y}^{i,j}\le D_{x,y-1}^{i,j}+1\) implies \(L_{x,y}^{i,j}\ge L_{x,y-1}^{i,j}\). First, we apply Lemma 3.16 to derive \(L_{x,y}^{i,j}\) for the two extreme values \(y\in\{b_{j-1}^Y,b_j^Y\}\). Next, for each value \(r\in[\lfloor\mathrm{log}_{1+\alpha} L_{x,b_{j-1}^Y}^{i,j}\rfloor\dots\lfloor\mathrm{log}_{1+\alpha} L_{x,b_j^Y}^{i,j}\rfloor]\), we binary search for the smallest \(y\in[b_{j-1}^Y\dots b_j^Y]\) such that \(\mathrm{log}_{1+\alpha} L_{x,y}^{i,j}\ge r\), and include _v<sub>x,y</sub>_ in **P**_<sub>i,j</sub>_. The binary searches are executed in parallel, with Lemma 3.16 applied to determine \(L_{x,y}^{i,j}\) for all the current pivots. This way, the algorithm is implemented in \(\widetilde{O}(1+\mathrm{log}_{1+\alpha} L_{x,b_j^Y}^{i,j}-\mathrm{log}_{1+\alpha} L_{y,b_{j-1}^Y,y}^{i,j}+|\mathbf{P}\cap\mathrm{in}^{B_{i,j}}|)\) time. Due to \(L_{y,b_{j-1}^Y}^{i,j}\ge L_{y,b_{j-1}^Y}^{i,j-1}\), the first term sums up to \(\widetilde{O}(\mathrm{log}_{1+\alpha}|Y|)=\widetilde{O}(\epsilon^{-1}(p_X+p_Y))\) across \(j\in[1\dots p_Y]\), and to \(\widetilde{O}(\epsilon^{-1}(p_X+p_Y)^2)\) across \(B_{i,j}\in\mathbf{B}\). This also bounds the number of portals created, so the second term, which sums up to |**P**| across all boxes, is also \(\widetilde{O}(\epsilon^{-1}(p_X+p_Y)^2)\).

_Proof of Theorem 3.14._ The algorithm uses Corollary 3.9 and Lemma 3.17. Due to \(p_X+p_Y=\frac{N+M}{\tau}\) , the overall running time is \(\widetilde{O}\big(nm\tau+\frac{(N+M)^2}{\epsilon\tau^2}\big)\). Optimizing \(\tau\), we get the running time of \(\widetilde{O}(nm+\epsilon^{-1}+(nm(N+M))^{2/3}\epsilon^{-1/3})\).

If the first term dominates, then \(nm\ge(nm(N+M))^{2/3}\epsilon^{-1/3}\ge(N+M)^2\epsilon^{-1}\). However, \(O(NM)=O((N+M)^2\epsilon^{-1})\) time is enough to compute LCS(_X,Y_) exactly without compression. If the second term dominates, then \(\epsilon^{-1}\ge(nm(N+M))^{2/3}\epsilon^{-1/3}\ge nm(N+M)\). However, \(\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{nm}(N+M))=\widetilde{O}(nm(N+M))\) time is enough to compute LCS(_X,Y_) exactly using Proposition 3.13 with _D=N+M_.

## 4 FPTAS For Compressed Median k-Edit Distance

The median _k_-edit distance is defined as below.

**Definition 4.1.** The (median) edit distance \(\delta_E(X_1,\dots,X_k)\) of _k_ strings _X_<sub>1</sub>_,...,X<sub>k</sub>_ is the minimum total number of edits (insertions, deletions, and substitutions) needed to make all strings _X<sub>i</sub>_ equal some string _X_<sup>∗</sup>. That is, \(\delta_E(X_1,\dots,X_k)=min_{X^*}\sum_{i=1}^k\delta_E(X_i,X^*)\).

For the (median) edit distance between _k_ strings, we show that allowing \((1+\epsilon)\)-approximation gives an algorithm circumventing the bound in Theorem 6.5:

**Theorem 4.2.** _Given k=O_(1) _straight-line programs_ **G**_<sub>X<sub>i</sub></sub> of total size n generating strings X<sub>i</sub> of total length N\>_0 _and a parameter_ \(\epsilon\in(0,1]\)_, an integer between_ \(\delta_E(X_1,\dots,X_k)\) _and_ \((1+\epsilon)\delta_E(X_1,\dots,X_k)\) _can be computed in_ \(\widetilde{O}\left(\epsilon^{-O(k)}n^{k/2}N^{k/2}\right)\) _time._

To prove the above theorem, we use a different set of techniques than in the two-string case. Most approaches for speeding up the textbook DP algorithm for two (compressible) strings, including the aforementioned results in this paper, rely on the ability to perform computations involving DIST matrices efficiently. These computations crucially depend on the fact that DIST matrices satisfy the Monge property. However, for the natural high-dimensional generalization of DIST matrices, we do not know of any analog of the Monge property they satisfy that allows us to perform similar computations even for three-string similarity problems. Indeed, most natural generalizations of the Monge property seem to not hold even in the three-string setting (see Section 9 for more details). Thus, it appears unlikely that, for example, an algorithm that partitions the DP table into boxes and computes the DP values on the boundary of each box using computations involving DIST matrices would be substantially more efficient than the textbook edit-distance algorithm, even in the three-string setting.

This motivates us to instead use the window-respecting alignment scheme that has appeared in approximation algorithms for edit distance (e.g., \[CDG<sup>+</sup>18, GRS20\]).

## 4.1 Window-Respecting Alignments

We will assume that \(\delta_E(X_1,\dots,X_k)\) lies between _D_ and 2_D_ for some known _D_ at the loss of a log_N_ factor in the runtime. We partition _X_<sub>1</sub> into \(\lceil|X_1|/\tau\rceil\) disjoint windows _W_<sub>1,1</sub> to \(W_{1,N/\tau}\) each of length \(\tau\) (without loss of generality; we could always e.g. pad each string with an equal amount of a new dummy character to ensure |_X_<sub>1</sub>| is a multiple of \(\tau\), without asymptotically affecting their size or compression size). That is, \(W_{1,j}=X_1[(j-1)\tau+1,j\tau]\).

We define for _X_<sub>2</sub>_,...,X<sub>k</sub>_ possibly overlapping windows indexed by (i) \(\Delta\), a guess for the (signed) difference between the length of _W_ and the corresponding window in _X_<sub>1</sub> and (ii) the starting position _p_ of the window. More formally, the windows are indexed by \(W_{i,\Delta,p}\). Throughout the section, let \(\sigma:=max\{\lfloor\epsilon D\tau/|X_1|\rfloor,1\}\) and _R<sub>d</sub>(x_) denote _x_ rounded down to the nearest multiple of \(\sigma\). Then \(W_{i,\Delta,p}=X_i[p\sigma+1\dots R_d(p\sigma+\tau+\Delta)]\) (or is the empty string "starting" at position \(p\sigma+1\) if \(R_d(min\{p\sigma+\tau+\Delta,|X_i|\})<p\sigma+1\)). If \(R_d(p\sigma+\tau+\Delta)>|X_1|\), \(W_{i,\Delta,p}\) is not included in our set of windows. We will define this window for:

• All \(\Delta\) in \(\{0,1,-1,\lfloor(1+\epsilon)\rfloor,-\lfloor(1+\epsilon)\rfloor,\lfloor(1+\epsilon)^2\rfloor,\dots\lfloor(1+\epsilon)^{\lceil log_{1+\epsilon} 2\tau/\epsilon^2\rceil}\rfloor\}\cup\{-\tau\}\) for which \(\tau+\Delta\ge 0\),<tbc>

• All _p_ from 0 to \(\lfloor|X_i|/\sigma\rfloor\).

It suffices to consider windows of size at most \(2\tau/\epsilon^2\) by the following lemma:

**Lemma 4.3.** _Given X_<sub>1</sub>_,X_<sub>2</sub>_,...,X<sub>k</sub> and a parameter_ \(\tau\)_, for_ \(J=|X_1|/\tau\)_, let X_<sup>∗</sup> _be the string such that_ \(\delta_E(X_1,X_2,\dots X_n)=\sum_i\delta_E(X_i,X^*)\)_. There exists a partition of each X_<sub>1</sub> _into substrings_ \(\{X_{1,j}\}_{j\in[J]}\)_, disjoint substrings of the other X<sub>i</sub>,_ \(\{X_{i,j}\}_{j\in[J]}\)_, and a partition of X_<sup>∗</sup> _into substrings_ \(\{X_j^*\}_{j\in[J]}\) _such that:_

• \(|X_{1,j}|=\tau\) _for all j._<tbc>

• _For any j and_ \(j<j'\)_, X<sub>i,j</sub> appears before_ \(X_{i,j^\prime}\) _in X<sub>i</sub>._<tbc>

• \(max_{i,j}|X_{i,j}|\le 2\tau/\epsilon^2\).<tbc>

• \(\sum_{j\in[J]}\delta_E(X_{ij},X_j^*)+|X_i|-\sum_{j\in[J]}|X_{i,j}|\le(1+3\epsilon)\delta_E(X_i,X^*),\)<tbc>

<tbc>_Which implies:_<tbc>

<tbc>\(\sum_{j\in[J]}\delta_E(X_{1,j},X_{2,j},\dots,X_{k,j})+\sum_{i>1}(|X_i|-\sum_{j\in[J]}|X_{i,j}|)\le(1+3\epsilon)\delta_E(X_1,X_2,\dots X_k).\)<tbc>

<tbc>_That is, the cost of the alignment that aligns X_<sub>1_,j_</sub> _with each X<sub>i,j</sub>, and then deletes all characters in X_<sub>2</sub> _to X<sub>k</sub> that are unaligned with some X_<sub>1_,j_</sub> _is at most_ \((1+3\epsilon)\delta_E(X_1,X_2,\dots X_k)\).

Effectively, Lemma 4.3 says that there is a near-optimal alignment that aligns the windows of _X_<sub>1</sub> to substrings of the other strings that are not more than \(1/\epsilon^2\) times larger.

_Proof._ We partition _X_<sub>1</sub> into substrings of length \(\tau\), \(\{X_{1,j}\}_{j\in[J]}\). _X_<sup>∗</sup> can be partitioned into substrings \(\{\tilde{X}_j^*\}_{j\in[J]}\) such that \(\delta_E(X_1,X^*)=\sum_{j\in[J]}\delta_E(X_{1,j},\tilde{X}_j^*)\).

First, we will "realign" _X_<sub>1</sub> and _X_<sup>∗</sup> to ensure no \(\tilde{X}_j^*\) is much larger than _X_<sub>1_,j_</sub>. Call a contiguous subsequence of \[_J_\], \([j..j']:=\{j,j+1,\dots j'\}\), "skewed" if \(\sum_{m\in[j..j^\prime]}|X_{1,m}|<\frac{\epsilon}{2}\sum_{m\in[j..j^\prime]}|\tilde{X}_m^*|\). Let us take a "maximal" set _S_ of disjoint skewed contiguous subsequences, i.e. a set _S_ such that (i) all the subsequences in _S_ are disjoint (ii) for every contiguous subsequence _s_ in _S_, there is no skewed contiguous subsequence \(s'\) such that \(s\subset s'\) and (iii) there is no skewed contiguous subsequence that is not in _S_ but also is completely disjoint from every element of _S_.

For each skewed contiguous subsequence \([j..j']\) in _S_, note that \(j'+1\) does not appear in any element of _S_ (otherwise, \([j..j']\) and this element can be combined to form a longer skewed contiguous subsequence, violating (ii)), and \([j..j'+1]\) is not skewed (again, \([j..j'+1]\) being skewed would violate (ii) since \([j..j']\subset[j..j'+1]\)). Take _S_ and replace each \([j..j']\) with \([j..j'+1]\) to get \(S'\). For each \([j..j'+1]\in S'\), we have:<tbc>

\(\frac{\epsilon}{2}\sum_{m\in[j..j^\prime+1]}|\tilde{X}_m^*|\le\sum_{m\in[j..j^\prime+1]}|X_{1,m}|\le 2\sum_{m\in[j..j^\prime]}|X_{1,m}|<\epsilon\sum_{m\in[j..j^\prime+1]}|\tilde{X}_m^*|.\) (1)

<tbc>The right-hand side of (1) implies:<tbc>

\(\delta_E(\circlearrowleft_{m\in[j..j^\prime+1]}X_{1,m},\circlearrowleft_{m\in[j..j^\prime+1]}\tilde{X}_m^*)\ge(1-\epsilon)|\circlearrowleft_{m\in[j..j^\prime+1]}\tilde{X}_m^*|.\)

<tbc>It also implies that for any partition of \(\circlearrowleft_{m\in[j..j^\prime+1]}\tilde{X}_m^*\) into substrings \(\{X_m^*\}_{m\in[j..j^\prime+1]}\), we have:<tbc>

\(\sum_{m\in[j..j^\prime+1]}\delta_E(X_{1,m},X_m^*)\le(1+\epsilon)|\circlearrowleft_{m\in[j..j^\prime+1]}\tilde{X}_m^*|.\)

<tbc>And so if \(\epsilon\) is sufficiently small:

\(\sum_{m\in\cup_{e\in S^\prime} e}\delta_E(X_{1,m},X_m^*)\le\frac{1+\epsilon}{1-\epsilon}\sum_{m\in\cup_{e\in S^\prime} e}\delta_E(X_{1,m},\tilde{X}_m^*)\le(1+3\epsilon)\sum_{m\in\cup_{e\in S^\prime} e}\delta_E(X_{1,m},\tilde{X}_m^*)\)

In particular, because of the left-hand side of (1), we can choose the partition of \(\circlearrowleft_{m\in[j..j^\prime+1]}\tilde{X}_m^*\) that splits it into substrings \(\{X_m^*\}_{m\in[j..j^\prime+1]}\), each of length at most \(2\tau/\epsilon\).

Now if we set \(X_m^*=\tilde{X}_m^*\) for any _m_ not in a subsequence in \(S'\), we trivially have:<tbc>

\(\sum_{m\notin\cup_{e\in S^\prime} e}\delta_E(X_{1,m},X_m^*)\le\sum_{m\notin\cup_{e\in S^\prime} e}\delta_E(X_{1,m},\tilde{X}_m^*)\)

<tbc>And also \(X_m^*\le 2\tau/\epsilon\) for all such _m_ (otherwise, _m_ should appear in some subsequence in \(S'\) by condition (iii)). So we’ve found a partition of _X_<sup>∗</sup> into substrings \(\{X_j^*\}_{j\in[J]}\) such that \(|X_j^*|\le\frac{1}{\epsilon}|X_{1,j}|\) for all _j_, and:<tbc>

\(\sum_{j\in[J]}\delta_E(X_{1,j},X_j^*)\le(1+3\epsilon)\sum_{j\in[J]}\delta_E(X_{1,j},\tilde{X}_j^*).\)

<tbc>Now, we will use this partition to determine \(\{X_{i,j}\}_{i>1,j\in[J]}\). For each _i_, _X<sub>i</sub>_ can be partitioned into substrings \(X'_{i,j}\) such that \(\delta_E(X_i,X^*)=\sum_{j\in[J]}\delta_E(X'_{i,j},X_j^*)\). If \(|X'_{i,j}|\le 2\tau/\epsilon^2\), we set \(X_{i,j}=X'_{i,j}\). If any \(X'_{i,j}\) has length larger than \(2\tau/\epsilon^2>|X_j^*|/\epsilon\), then \(\delta_E(X'_{i,j},X_j^*)\ge(1-\epsilon)|X'_{i,j}|\). On the other hand:

\(\delta_E(\gamma,X_j^*)+|X'_{i,j}|\le(1+\epsilon)|X'_{i,j}|\le\frac{1+\epsilon}{1-\epsilon}\delta_E(X'_{i,j},X_j^*)\le(1+3\epsilon)\delta_E(X'_{i,j},X_j^*)\)

for the empty string \(\gamma\). So we can now choose _X<sub>i,j</sub>_ to be any empty substring of \(X'_{i,j}\). These choices of _X<sub>i,j</sub>_ give the properties of the lemma, completing the proof.

Let W<sub>1</sub> be the set of all windows we partition _X_<sub>1</sub> into, and W_<sub>i</sub>_ be the set of windows we define for _X<sub>i</sub>_. Let `s`(_W_) denote the index of the first character in _W_, and `e`(_W_) denote the index of the last character. For _k_ strings, we define a window-respecting alignment as follows:

Our algorithm solves the following dynamic program: \(c(x_1,x_2,\dots x_k)=min\left\{\begin{array}{ c } min_{i\neq 1}c(x_1,x_2,\dots,x_i-\sigma,\dots,x_k)+\sigma \\ min_{W_1,\dots W_k\in\mathcal{W}_1\times\cdots\times\mathcal{W}_k:\forall_i\mathsf{e}(W_i)=x_i,W_1=\cdots=W_k}[c(\mathsf{s}(W_1)-1,\dots,\mathsf{s}(W_k)-1)] \\ min_{W_1,\dots W_k\in\mathcal{W}_1\times\cdots\times\mathcal{W}_k:\forall_i\mathsf{e}(W_i)=x_i}[c(\mathsf{s}(W_1)-1,\dots,\mathsf{s}(W_k)-1) \\ +min_{d\in\mathcal{D}}\delta_E(\mathtt{shift}_d(W_1),\dots,\mathtt{shift}_d(W_k))] \end{array}\right.\) For every _k_-tuple such that _x_1 is a multiple of \(\tau\), _x_2_,...,xk_ are all multiples of \(\sigma\), and such that \(|x_i-x_1|\le 4D\) for all _i_.

At a high-level, in steps 1 and 2 of _k_-ED-Alg we exploit the compression of the input strings to identify a small set of "representative" strings for each _Xi_, such that for each window in _Xi_ there is a representative string within small edit distance of that window. In step 3, we then compute the median distance between _k_-tuples of representative strings (instead of between all _k_-tuples of windows). Since all windows are within a small distance of some representative string, this also gives for all _k_-tuples of windows a reasonable approximation of their median distance. Step 4 of _k_-ED-Alg uses these approximations to solve a natural DP for finding an optimal window-respecting alignment. This DP is the same as the standard DP for edit distance, but instead of matching characters we are only allowed to match windows, at cost equal to (the approximation of) their median distance. We first bound the runtime of _k_-ED-Alg. The following lemmas show that Steps 1 and 2 of _k_-ED-Alg can be performed efficiently (as well as their correctness): **Lemma 4.6.** _Given a straight-line program_ **G** _of size n that generates a string X of size n, a length parameter_ \(\tau\)_, and a parameter_ \(\delta_\mathrm{max}\le\tau\)_, there exists an algorithm that in time O_(|_X_|) _finds (an implicit representation of) a set S of_ \(O(n\tau/\delta_\mathrm{max})\) _substrings of length at most_ \(\tau\) _such that for every length_ \(\tau\) _substring of X, x, there is a string `shift`(x_) _in S such that_ \(\delta_E(x,\mathtt{\textit{shift}}(x))\le\delta_\mathrm{max}\)_. \(\delta_\mathrm{max}\) of some string in this set. So adding these strings to _S_ gives that _S_ now has size at most \(3n\tau/\delta_\mathrm{max}\) and has the desired properties.

For an efficient implementation of this procedure, we can compute the optimal LZ77 factorization in _O_(|_X_|) time \[RPE81\]. Our framework for the algorithm is similar to the framework from the previous section which uses window-respecting alignments. Our algorithm will actually solve a more general problem of computing an approximation of a set of values which we call the _edit tuples_. We again assume \(\delta_{CE}(X_1,\dots,X_k)\) lies between _D_ and 2_D_ for some known (power of 2) _D_. **Definition 5.3.** Given strings _X_1_,X_2_,...,Xk_, an edit tuple of these strings is a vector \(v\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^k\) such that there exists _X_∗ for which \(\delta_E(X_i,X^*)\le v_i\) for all _i_. ## 5.1 Approximation Guarantee

We first prove the approximation guarantee of _k_-CED-Alg, as it will be necessary for our runtime analysis to specify what choice of \(\epsilon_0\) to \(\epsilon_\ell\) is needed for the desired approximation guarantee.

**Lemma 5.5.** _Let the sequence_ \(\epsilon_0,\dots,\epsilon_\ell\) _satisfy_ \(\epsilon_0\le 1\) _and_ \(\epsilon_{m+1}=\frac{1}{16k}\epsilon_m\) _for all m. Then at level m of the recursion, each invocation of k_-CED-Alg(\(X'_1,X'_2,\dots,X'_k\)_, d, m) returns a set of edit tuples that is a_ \((\epsilon_md+\frac{\epsilon_mD\tau_m}{|X_1|})\)_-approximation of_ \(\mathtt{top}_{2d}(X'_1,\dots,X'_k)\).

_Proof._ We proceed by induction. Clearly the guarantee holds for the base case \(m=\ell\), since we solve the base cases using exact algorithms.

Inductively, assuming at level _m_+1, any edit tuple generated returned by _k_-CED-Alg is element-wise greater than some edit tuple of the corresponding windows, by an argument similar to the first part of the proof of Lemma 5.4 the same property holds at level _m_. So we just need to show that each edit tuple returned by _k_-CED-Alg is not too large an overestimate of some edit tuple of its input strings.

Take any edit tuple _v_ for any window-respecting alignment _f_. Assume the approximation guarantee holds for calls made at level _m_+1. We show that for the corresponding path through the DP table for _c_, there is a vector close to _v_ in the edit tuples generated by this path. _v_ can be decomposed as \(\sum_{j\in[J]}v_j+r(f)\) where _v<sub>j</sub>_ is an edit tuple of _f(W_<sub>1_,j_</sub>). Let _d<sub>j</sub>_ be the smallest value in D such that \(d_j\ge||v_j||_\infty\). By our inductive hypothesis, for each _j_ we get a \((\epsilon_{m+1}d_j+\frac{\epsilon_{m+1}D\tau_{m+1}}{|X_1|})\)-approximation of the edit tuples of `top`<sub>_d<sub>j</sub>_</sub>(_f(W_<sub>1_,j_</sub>)) from the call to _k_-CED-Alg(_f(W_<sub>1_,j_</sub>)_,d<sub>j</sub>,m_+1), which includes a vector \(v'_j\) that is element-wise at most \(v_j+(\epsilon_{m+1}d_j+\frac{\epsilon_{m+1}D\tau_{m+1}}{|X_1|})\cdot\mathbf{1}\le v_j+(2\epsilon_{m+1}||v_j||_\infty+\frac{\epsilon_{m+1}D\tau_{m+1}}{|X_1|})\) if \(\epsilon\) is sufficiently small. In addition, the sum of the vectors contributed by the first case in the recurrence relation for _c_ is _r(f_). So there is an edit tuple computed by our algorithm for this path that is element-wise less than:

\(\sum_j[v_j+(2\epsilon_{m+1}||v_j||_\infty+\frac{\epsilon_{m+1}D\tau_{m+1}}{|X_1|})\cdot\mathbf{1}]+r(f)\le v+\left(4\epsilon_{m+1}kd+\frac{\epsilon_{m+1}D\tau_m}{|X_1|}\right)\cdot\mathbf{1}.\)

There are _O_(log_d_) choices of _d_ and \(O(log_{1+\epsilon_\ell}(2\tau_\ell/\epsilon_\ell^2))=O(log^{O(1)}(N)/\epsilon^2)\) possible sizes for each choice of _d_, so there are \(O(log^{O(k)}(N)/\epsilon^{2k})\) different tuples of possible window sizes<tbc>

The proof of Lemma 4.6 implies that for any string _X_ generated by an SLP of size _n_, the number of distinct substrings of length \(\tau\) is \(O(n\tau)\) (in particular, in that proof when \(\delta=1\) we are simply taking every substring into _S_). Besides base-cases, the only work our algorithm does is rounding and convolutions. We can perform the recursion in an amortized fashion. That is, we never make multiple calls to _k_-CED-Alg on the same _k_-tuple of strings with the same choice of _d_. Similarly, for each _d_ and each level _m_+1 call to _k_-CED-Alg, we only round that call’s output’s coordinates to the nearest multiple of \(\sigma_m(d)\) once. The time spent rounding a set of vectors is proportional to its size, and the final set of vectors that we round was produced by a convolution that took time at least the size of the set of vectors. For this convolution, with amortization we only need to round its output at most log_N_ times, once per value of _d_ in D. Thus, the time spent on rounding is bounded by the time spent on convolutions times _O_(log_N_).

We now just need to bound the time spent on convolutions. Fix a level _m_ of the recursion and a choice of _d_ in the input. We will bound the total work across all calls at level _m_ and with _d_ as input; there are _O_(log_N_) levels and _O_(loglog_N_) levels, so our final bound on time spent on convolutions will be within logarithmic factors of the bound for one choice of _m_ and _d_.

The time spent on convolutions in any call is bounded by a constant factor times the time spent on convolutions in the second case in the recurrence relation, i.e., convolutions involving recursive calls. We perform these convolutions on tuples in {0,1_,...,_3_d_} whose coordinates are multiples of \(\sigma_m(d)\), i.e., have size at most \(O((d/\sigma_m(d))^k)=O((\tau_m/\epsilon_{m+1}\tau_{m+1})^k)=O(N^{o(k)}/\epsilon^k)\). So the time spent on convolutions per call to _k_-CED-Alg is \(N^{o(k)}/\epsilon^{O(k)}\) as well.

We now just need to bound the number of calls made to _k_-CED-Alg, and our final runtime will be within an \(N^{o(k)}/\epsilon^{O(k)}\) factor of this. We bound the number of calls at each level in two ways. The second way is exactly what we did in Section 4 to bound the number of coordinates in the DP table: For every _k_-tuple of windows we call _k_-CED-Alg on at level _m_ with parameter _d_, the window \(X'_1\) ends at an index in _X_<sub>1</sub> that is a multiple of \(\tau_m\), and the other windows end at indices in _X_<sub>2</sub>_,...,X<sub>k</sub>_ that are multiples of \(\sigma_m(d)\). The desired bound of \(O(n^{k/2}\cdot N^{k/2+o(k)}/\epsilon^{O(k)})\) calls follows by taking the geometric mean of the first and second bound, which is at least the smaller of the two.

## 6.2 Lower Bound with LCS

In this section we will argue that if we have _k_ strings each of length _M_ and they have a SLP compression of size _m_ then the problem requires _M_<sup>_k_-1-_o_(1)</sup>_m_<sup>1-_o_(1)</sup> if SETH is true. The core of this section is building a generalized "perfect alignment" gadget. This is a gadget that causes substrings to be aligned with no skips or merges. We use this generalized alignment gadget to generalize the work of \[ABBK17\]. The main idea for this perfect alignment gadget is that between every string we want to align, we add symbols $<sub>1</sub>$<sub>2</sub>_..._$_<sub>k</sub>_. Additionally, at the end of each string _S<sub>i</sub>_ in our gadget, we add many copies of these characters, excepting $_<sub>i</sub>_. That is, we add $<sub>1</sub>_..._$<sub>_i_-1</sub>$<sub>_i_+1</sub>_..._$_<sub>k</sub>_. Via this construction, any valid perfect alignment will match all available copies of $_<sub>i</sub>_ for all _i_. Any alignment that isn’t perfect (for example it skips matching some sub-string in the middle of _S<sub>i</sub>_) will miss out on one of these $_<sub>i</sub>_ characters in _S<sub>i</sub>_, thus lowering the value of a potential _k_-LCS.

## 6.6 Easy Edit Distance Lower Bounds from LCS

In this section we will prove that _k_-median edit distance is hard from \(k'\)-LCS. We take a \(k'\)-LCS instance and add various numbers of empty strings. **Definition 6.17.** Given _k_ strings _S_<sub>1</sub>_,...,S<sub>k</sub>_ of lengths _M_<sub>1</sub>_,M_<sub>2</sub>_,...,M<sub>k</sub>_ the _k_-edit distance (or _k_-median edit distance) of those strings is the minimum sum across all strings of edits needed to make all strings equal some new string \(S'\). ## 6.8 Center Edit Distance

Nicolas and Rivals present a very simple reduction from a specific version of (_k_-1)-LCS to _k_-Center Edit Distance. This reduction simply adds the empty string as the last string.
